newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Last of Colombia's Ochoa Clan freed from prison.
newsitem.headline: Last of Colombia's Ochoa Clan freed from prison.

text.p: The last member of the so-called Ochoa Clan of Colombian drug traffickers still in prison regained his freedom on Monday after less than six years behind bars, authorities said.

Fabio Ochoa Vasquez, 36 and the youngest of three brothers who shot to notoriety through their exploits with the violent Medellin drug cartel, was released from the Itagui prison in northwest Colombia on Monday afternoon, prison officials said.

Before climbing into an armour-plated Mitsubishi jeep and speeding away from the jail, Ochoa told reporters he had no fear of extradition to the United States and planned to devote the rest of his life to raising his children.
"I believe in Colombian laws," he said, apparently referring to the country's five-year-old ban on extradition.

His release followed that of his oldest brother, Jorge Luis Ochoa Vasquez on July 5 and Juan David Ochoa on July 29. All three had been held in the Itagui prison on the outskirts of Medellin, and all served less than six years behind bars.

The three, purported multi-millionaires who once topped wanted lists worldwide, were given light prison sentences because they surrendered and confessed to drug-related crimes. They were considered leading members of the Medellin cartel headed by Pablo Escobar, the notoriously violent drug boss who was gunned down by police in December 1993.

A policy of short prison sentences for top Colombian traffickers was introduced under President Ernesto Samper's predecessor, Cesar Gaviria. It is known as "the policy of submission" and has been severely criticised by the United States.
Samper has vowed to stiffen penalties for traffickers in legislation pending before Congress, but the reforms have been dismissed as too little, too late by U.S. drug experts.

Juan David Ochoa has been linked by U.S. drug agents to the February 1986 killing in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, of Barry Seal, a Medellin cartel associate who became a valuable informant for the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.

No murder charges were ever filed against Juan David and none of the Ochoa brothers were held directly responsible for the campaign of bombings, assassinations and kidnappings that Escobar waged in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
The bloody campaign was unleashed to press the government into banning the extradition of drug lords to the United States -- a prohibition that was written into Colombia's Consititution in 1991.
